readings.c1s1: results, relating to strong as well as weak variations, are obtained by a method which permits of the expression of the variation of an integral as a line integral taken along the varied curve. Let <math>\text{A}</math>, <math>\text{B}</math> be the end points, and let the stationary curve <math>\text{AB}</math> be drawn. If the end points <math>\text{A}</math>, <math>\text{B}</math> are not a pair of conjugate points, and if the point conjugate to <math>\text{A}</math> does not lie on the arc <math>\text{AB}</math>, then we may find a point <math>\text{A}'</math>, on the backward continuation of the stationary curve <math>\text{BA}</math> beyond <math>\text{A}</math>, so near to <math>\text{A}</math> that the point conjugate to <math>\text{A}'</math> lies on the forward continuation of the arc <math>\text{AB}</math> beyond <math>\text{B}</math>. This being the case, it is possible to delimit an area of finite breadth, so that the arc <math>\text{AB}</math> of the stationary curve joining <math>\text{A}</math>, <math>\text{B}</math> lies entirely within the area, and {{smaller|'''''Field of stationary curves.'''''}} no two stationary curves drawn through <math>\text{A}'</math> intersect within the area. Through any point of such an area it is possible to draw one, and only one, stationary curve which passes through <math>\text{A}'</math>. This family of stationary curves is said to constitute a ''field'' of stationary curves about the curve <math>\text{AB}</math>. We suppose that such a field exists, and that the varied curve <math>\text{AQPB}</math> lies entirely within the delimited area. The variation of the integral <math>\int\text{F}(x,\ y,\ y')dx</math> is identical with the line integral of <math>\text{F}</math> taken round a contour consisting of the varied curve <math>\text{AQPB}</math> and the stationary curve <math>\text{AB}</math>, in the sense <math>\text{AQPBA}</math>. The line integral may, as usual, be replaced by the sum of line integrals taken round a series of cells, the external boundaries of the set of cells being identical with the

readings.c1s3:
''General expression for variation of an integral.''

Let <math>\text{Q}</math>, <math>\text{P}</math> be points on the varied curve, and let <math>\text{A}'\text{Q}</math>, <math>\text{A}'\text{P}</math> be the stationary curves of the field which pass through <math>\text{Q}</math>, <math>\text{P}</math>. Let <math>\text{P}</math> follow <math>\text{Q}</math> in the sense <math>\text{AQPB}</math> in which the varied curve is described. Then the contour consisting of the stationary curve <math>\text{A}'\text{Q}</math>, from <math>\text{A}'</math> to <math>\text{Q}</math>, the varied curve <math>\text{QP}</math>, from <math>\text{Q}</math> to <math>\text{P}</math>, and the stationary curve <math>\text{A}'\text{P}</math>, from <math>\text{P}</math> to <math>\text{A}'</math>, is the boundary of a cell (fig. 4). Let us denote the integral of <math>\text{F}</math> taken along a stationary curve by round brackets, thus <math>(\text{A}'\text{Q})</math>, and the integral of <math>\text{F}</math> taken along any other curve by square brackets, thus <math>[\text{PQ}]</math>. If the varied curve is divided into a number of arcs such as <math>\text{QP}</math> we have the result
{{block center|<math>[\text{AQPB}]-(\text{AB}) = \Sigma\{(\text{A}'\text{Q})+[\text{QP}]-(\text{A}'\text{P})\},</math>}}
and the right-hand member can be expressed as a line integral taken along the varied curve <math>\text{AQPB}</math>.

To effect this transformation we seek an approximate expression for the term <math>(\text{A}'\text{Q})+[\text{QP}]-(\text{A}'\text{P})</math>

''Sufficient and necessary conditions.'' Further, we may specialize the excess function by identifying <math>\text{A}'</math> with <math>\text{A}</math>, and calculating the function for a point <math>\text{P}</math> on the arc <math>\text{AB}</math> of the stationary curve <math>\text{AB}</math>, and an arbitrary direction of the tangent at <math>\text{P}</math> to the varied curve. This process is equivalent to the introduction of a particular type of strong variation. We may in fact take, as a varied curve, the arc <math>\text{AQ}</math> of a neighbouring stationary curve, the straight line <math>\text{QP}</math> drawn from <math>\text{Q}</math> to a point of the arc <math>\text{AB}</math>, and the arc <math>\text{PB}</math> of the stationary curve <math>\text{AB}</math> (fig. 6). The sign of the variation is then the
readings.c2s2: same as that of the function <math>\text{E}(x,\ y,\ \tan\phi,\ \tan\psi)</math>, where <math>(x,\ y)</math> is the point <math>\text{P}</math>, <math>\psi</math> is the angle which the straight line <math>\text{OP}</math> makes with the
readings.c2s3:
axis of <math>x</math>, and <math>\phi</math> is the angle which the tangent at P to the curve APB makes with the same axis. We thus arrive at a new ''necessary'' (but not sufficient) condition for the existence of an extremum of the integral <math>\int\text{F}ds</math>, viz. the specialized excess function, so calculated, must not change sign between A and B.

'''''Developments connected with the excess function.'''''

The sufficient condition, and the new necessary condition, associated with the excess function, as well as the expression for the variation as <math>\int\text{E}ds</math>, are due to Weierstrass. In applications to special problems it is generally permissible to identify A′ with A, and to regard QP as straight. The direction of QP must be such that the integral of <math>\text{F}</math> taken along it is finite and real. We shall describe such directions as ''admissible.'' In the statement of the sufficient condition, and the new necessary condition, it is of course understood that the direction specified by <math>\psi</math> is admissible. The excess function generally vanishes if <math>\psi=\phi</math>, but it does not change sign. It can be shown without difficulty that, when <math>\psi</math> is very nearly equal to <math>\phi</math>, the sign of <math>\text{E}</math> is the same as that of
{{block center|<math>(\tan\psi-\tan\phi)^2\cos\phi\left(\frac{\partial^2\text{F}}{\partial y'^2}\right)_{y'=\tan\phi}</math>}}
and thus the necessary condition as to the sign of the excess function includes Legendre's condition as to the sign of <math>\partial^1\text{F}/\partial y'^2</math>.

Weierstrass's conditions have been obtained by D. Hilbert from the observation that, if <math>p</math> is a function of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, the integral
{{block center|<math>\int\left\{\text{F}(x,y,p)+(y'-p)\left(\frac{\partial\text{F}}{\partial y'}\right)_{y'=p}\right\}dx</math>,}}
taken along a curve joining two fixed points, has the same value for all such curves, provided that there is a field of stationary curves, and that <math>p</math> is the gradient at the point <math>(x,\ y)</math> of that stationary curve of the field which passes through this point.

An instructive example of the excess function, and the conditions connected with it, is afforded by the integral
readings.c2s4:
<math>\int y^2y'^{-2}dx</math> or <math>\int y^2\dot{x}^3\dot{y}^{-2}d\theta</math>.

'''''Example of the excess function.'''''

The first integral of the principal equation is

{{block center|<math>y^2\dot{x}^2\dot{y}^{-2} = \text{const.}</math>,}}

and the stationary curves include the axis of <math>x</math>, straight lines parallel to the axis of <math>y</math>, and the family of exponential curves <math>y = ae^{cx}</math>. A field of stationary curves is expressed by the equation

{{block center|<math>y = y_0 \exp \{c(x-x_0)\}</math>,}}

and, as these have no envelope other than the initial point <math>(x_0, y_0)</math>, there are no conjugate points. The function <math>f_1</math> is <math>6\dot{x}\dot{y}^{-4}</math>, and this is positive for curves going from the initial point in the positive direction of the axis of <math>x</math>. The value of the excess function is

{{block center|<math>y^2\cos\psi(\cot^2\psi - 3\cot^2\phi + 2\tan\psi\cot^3\phi)</math>.}}

The directions <math>\psi = 0</math> and <math>\psi = \pi</math> are inadmissible. On putting <math>\psi = \tfrac{1}{2}\pi</math> we get <math>2y^2\cot^3\phi</math>; and on putting <math>\psi = \tfrac{3}{2}\pi</math> we get <math>-2y^2\cot^3\phi</math>. Hence the integral taken along AQ′PB is greater than that taken along APB, and the integral taken along AQPB is less than that taken along APB, when Q′Q are sufficiently near to P on the ordinate of P (fig. 7). {{block center|<math>(\text{A}'\text{Q})-(\text{A}'\text{P}) = -\Delta s.\cos\psi \left\{ \text{F}(x,y,p) + (\tan\psi - p)\frac{\partial\text{F}}{\partial p} \right\}_{p=\tan\phi}</math>}}
